title: Japanese Money Methods
note:
THE SALARY MONTH, US register. Ten scenes and only two drawn layers, which
     is the density chapter 1 of the -hi cut was approved at: the photographs are
     doing the work and everything proposed on top of them was a redrawing.

     Ground arc: cool screen-light at the notification -> green on the promise ->
     red through the bills -> warm on the small discretionary things -> neutral
     as they are counted -> red at the 20th and again where the money went ->
     warm on the question the chapter closes with.

     Archetypes: A A A B D D B A D A. Four layers assert what the stills cannot,
     and none of them draws its own photograph: the notification ARRIVING (s1,
     Lottie), six months of cover against the one that was budgeted (s4), a
     COUNT of forty-four (s6), the 20th being ringed while the balance drains
     (s7, Lottie + measure), and a drain with no single large stream (s9).

s1.comment:
1.1 · A · LOTTIE · no role · cool — frame 0 of the video, and the first half
     of a 11.924s HOLD that s2 finishes. The phone and the counter are present
     at frame 0 and ONLY the notification animates in (the asset's layer 7 is
     opacity 0 until frame 24, 100 at frame 27). That is the beat no still can
     hold: the money ARRIVING, rather than money having arrived.
motion:
/* THE HOLD, part 1 of 2. s1 and s2 are one object and one push; s2 carries an
   identical element driven from the SAME absolute times, so the two are
   pixel-identical through the 0.45s cross-dissolve and there is nothing for
   it to ghost against. (-hi ch1 gets this for free by hanging one phone off
   #root across both scenes on its own track; a chapter.json spec has no hook
   for root-level markup, and creating a `clip` from script would be invisible
   to the linter and to the renderer's DOM scan. Two synchronised instances is
   the version that survives the generator.)

   ONE pass at TRUE speed (180f / 30fps = 6.00s), then it holds on its last
   frame while the push keeps moving. -hi plays the loop twice because it has
   no other motion; here that would say the deposit landed a second time at
   6.8s, which is not true. Notification in at 0.80s, buzz again at 3.60s,
   still lit when s2 dissolves over it. */
var phone = loadLottie("#s1-phone", L_phone_on_counter_night);
/* lottie-web writes preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"; the artwork is 3:2 on
   a 16:9 stage, so `meet` pillarboxes it. `slice` is background-size:cover for
   an SVG. A property of THIS asset's aspect ratio, not of loadLottie. */
phone.renderer.svgElement.setAttribute("preserveAspectRatio", "xMidYMid slice");
playLottie(phone, S.s1, 6.00);
/* plateKen, not ken: pure scale, no xPercent drift, so the zoom CONTINUES
   across the cut instead of restarting. s1 reaches 1.10 at 4.039 — the exact
   frame s2 starts from — rather than at 4.489, so the handoff is exact and
   only the fading-out copy is briefly static. These are the cut's own numbers
   for #s1-bg / #s2-bg, moved onto the object that is actually visible. */
plateKen("#s1-phone", S.s1, 4.039, 1.00, 1.10);

s2.comment:
1.2 · A · LOTTIE · fund · green — the promise, and the second half of the
     hold. Same object, same instant, the push picked up at exactly 1.10 where
     s1 leaves it. The notification has faded by ~5.7s and the phone simply
     sits there for the rest of the line, which is the correct read: it landed
     once and it is already past.

s3.comment:
1.3 · A · PLATE · warn · red — a pile of bills IS the line; a drawn bill on
     top of it would trace it.

s4.comment:
1.4 · B · FIGURE · no role · neutral — THE SIX-MONTH BILL. The claim in the
     copy is "six months where you budgeted one", so the art is ONE cell against
     SIX, to the same scale, and nothing else. The previous 6-lit-of-10 read as
     a published proportion with a denominator that appears nowhere in the
     script (editor en-ch1-3 finding 9). The underlines are measurement rules,
     not decoration — they replace the stray red 62x8 mark that read as nothing.
     Plate geometry (p-b, 0 0 860 610), the cell rect (62x138 on a 76 pitch) and
     the baseline y are all unchanged; only the count and the spacing moved.

s5.comment:
1.5 · A · PLATE · no role · warm — one gift, two orders, one renewal. Gift
     bags photographed; a drawn count of four here would be a caption.

s6.comment:
1.6 · A · PLATE + COUNT · no role · neutral — every one small, every one
     fair. Forty-four identical slips on a strict 11x4 grid: uniform rects so
     the layer reads as a TALLY, which is the line's actual claim, and not as a
     second drawing of whatever receipts the photograph shows. A `.band` at
     z 0 darkens BEHIND them (rule 9 — the photograph itself is never graded
     per scene). Ported from -hi ch1, where the same band exists but is dead
     code: that scene is `art-off centred`, so its plate never renders.

s7.comment:
1.7 · B · FIGURE + LOTTIE · warn · red — BY THE 20th. The measure bar drains
     to almost nothing and the month grid burns down to a ringed 20th, on the
     same cue: one claim, two readings of it. The scene is no longer `centred` —
     B's right half now holds art, so the split is a layout again rather than a
     hole, and the type takes the left column with the vrule back on.

s8.comment:
1.8 · A · PLATE · no role · cool — YOU GO LOOKING. Hands on a printed
     statement; the search is the picture.

s9.comment:
1.9 · D · BAND · warn · deep red — IT IS NOT THERE. Twenty-four holes, each
     leaking a little, none of them large. Opacities raised throughout: the
     streams were `.6` inside a container the global `.art-forward` rule pins
     to `.52 !important`, so they rendered at .31 and vanished in the encode
     (editor en-ch1-3 finding 8). The container is lifted to .78 by id in the
     chapter css and the streams now carry no opacity of their own at all.
motion: for (var h = 0; h < 24; h++) tl.fromTo("#s9-p" + h, { scaleY: 0, transformOrigin: "50% 0%" }, { scaleY: 1, duration: 0.9, ease: "power1.in" }, S.s9 + 1.60 + (h % 6) * 0.1 + Math.floor(h / 6) * 0.09);
